extracted.intended_audience: researchers in computational humor, natural language processing, and machine learning (deep learning/RNNs)
extracted.subtask_description: Investigating whether machine learning models (notably neural networks/RNNs) can learn and represent the abstractions and mechanisms postulated by literary theories of humour, focusing on mechanism identification rather than binary humor classification.

rubrics_metrics.name: Identify abstractions predicted by literary theories of humour
rubrics_metrics.description: Automatically identify abstractions that are predicted to be relevant by established literary theories about the mechanisms of humor.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The paper's stated aim is to test whether an algorithm can 'identify abstractions' that literary theory suggests are important; evaluation should therefore assess whether learned representations correspond to those theory-predicted abstractions. Emphasis is on matching algorithmic abstractions to theoretical constructs rather than on surface-level features or labels.

rubrics_metrics.name: Algorithmic 'understanding' of humour
rubrics_metrics.description: Testing whether an algorithm — namely, a neural network — can "understand" humour.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluation should consider whether the model exhibits internal representations or behaviors that indicate comprehension of humor mechanisms/triggers. The authors use neural networks (deep learning, recurrent neural networks, dimensionality-reduction techniques) as the testbed; assessments should examine learned representations and whether they capture mechanism-like structure rather than only task performance metrics.

rubrics_metrics.name: Focus on underlying mechanisms and triggers rather than binary humour classification
rubrics_metrics.description: Do not focus on distinguishing humorous from serious statements; instead, identify the underlying mechanisms and triggers postulated by literary theories and verify if similar mechanisms can be learned by machines.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The authors explicitly state that binary humor detection is outside their focus (noting it's difficult even for humans). Evaluations and experiments should therefore be designed to probe mechanism-level hypotheses (e.g., incongruity, script-based triggers) and not only to optimize classification accuracy. This scope/limitation should guide dataset selection, task formulation, and interpretation of results.
